title: Conduct fumigation processes for structural pests

lessons.title: Tarping and sealing a structure
lessons.html:
The practical task

Structural fumigation is used for drywood termites, wood borers in roof timbers and furniture, stored product insects in mills and food factories, and quarantine treatment of containers and wood packaging. This module focuses on the practical steps of conducting the fumigation once the plan has been approved and the site prepared. All work is done by, or under the direct supervision of, an operator registered for fumigation under Act 36 of 1947, using a fumigant registered for the pest and situation.

Choosing the enclosure method

MethodWhen used
Whole-structure tarpingHouses and buildings with many gaps, such as old roofs; heritage buildings
Taping and sealingWell-built rooms, mills or warehouses where openings can be sealed from inside and outside
Sheeted enclosuresFurniture, pallets of wooden items or equipment fumigated under sheets on site
Containers and chambersWood packaging, export goods, items brought to a fixed fumigation facility

Tarping procedure

  1. Inspect all tarpaulins for holes and worn seams and repair them.
  2. Protect sharp roof edges, gutters and aerials with padding so sheets are not torn.
  3. Lift sheets onto the roof with enough people and safe access; never work on fragile roofs or near overhead power lines without proper controls.
  4. Overlap adjoining sheets generously and roll and clamp the joins to make them gas-tight.
  5. Seal the bottom edges to the ground with sand snakes or water snakes. On soil, wet the soil or lay sheeting so gas does not escape through it.
  6. Seal around obstacles such as pipes and plants.
  7. Secure sheets against wind with ropes as the plan requires.

Sealing from inside

Where sealing is used, tape every door edge, window, vent, extractor, conduit, drain and gap, from the inside where possible, and seal external openings. Check the roof space and eaves. Open interior doors, cupboards and drawers so gas reaches all parts of the structure. Place fans where the plan or label calls for gas distribution.

Final checks before introduction

Check that sampling lines are in place, warning signs are posted, the occupancy check is complete and signed, and the team is briefed. Weather must be suitable; strong wind increases leakage through sheets.

lessons.title: Introducing the fumigant and running the exposure
lessons.html:
Calculating the dose

Calculate the volume of the enclosed space. For a house under tarps, use the external dimensions including the roof space. Apply the label dose for the target pest, fumigant and temperature, and confirm the minimum exposure period. Have a second registered person check the calculation. Record the volume, dose rate, total quantity and temperature.

Introducing the fumigant

  • Gas from cylinders, such as sulfuryl fluoride where registered, is introduced through a hose from outside the enclosure, often into the airstream of a fan to aid mixing. Weigh the cylinder before and after to confirm the quantity released.
  • Solid phosphide formulations are placed on trays or in dispensers as the label directs, spread out so they do not heap, away from liquids, and positioned so the residues can be recovered. Applicators enter only with the respiratory protection the label specifies, work in pairs and exit quickly, with a standby person outside.

After introduction, seal the final opening and record the time.

Monitoring the exposure

  1. Read concentrations at each sampling line at the planned intervals.
  2. Record readings, time, temperature and weather.
  3. Monitor the perimeter and nearby buildings for leaks, especially downwind.
  4. Maintain guarding or patrols and keep signage in place.
  5. Respond to falling concentrations by finding and fixing leaks.

Never shorten the exposure period. If the target concentration cannot be held, consult your technical manager.

Remember the hazards

Fumigants such as sulfuryl fluoride have no warning odour, so detection depends on instruments. Phosphine's smell, when present, is not a reliable warning and may be absent at hazardous concentrations.

lessons.title: Ending the fumigation and handing back
lessons.html:
Aeration

  1. Confirm the full exposure has been completed.
  2. Check wind direction and keep the exclusion zone in place.
  3. Begin aeration from outside where possible: lift the downwind tarps first or open sealed vents, then work around the structure.
  4. Use fans as planned to clear the gas.
  5. Applicators who must enter wear the respiratory protection the label requires and work in pairs with a standby person.

Clearance

Test the air in every room, in roof spaces, cupboards and furniture, using an instrument suited to the fumigant. Clearance is only given when all readings are below the re-entry level on the label. Continue aeration where any reading is high; soft furnishings and mattresses can hold gas.

Residues and equipment

Recover phosphide residues and handle them as the label directs; they may still contain active material. Remove tape and sheets, inspect and fold them, and check the property for damage. Remove sampling lines.

Hand-back

  • Issue the clearance certificate with date, time and readings.
  • Remove warning signs only after clearance.
  • Brief the client on the result, any precautions and the follow-up inspection date.
  • Recommend preventive measures: timber replacement, treated timber, moisture correction or proofing.
  • Complete the fumigation record.

Key points

  • Inspect and repair tarpaulins, overlap and clamp joins and seal edges with snakes.
  • Calculate the dose from the enclosed volume and label, and have it checked.
  • Introduce fumigant from outside where possible; enter only in pairs with protection and a standby person.
  • Rely on instruments, not smell, and never shorten the exposure.
  • Clear only when all readings are below the label re-entry level, then certify and hand back.
